974.title: Frances of Rome (9 March)
974.hook: a wife and mother in Rome who cared for the sick in plague years
974.howItsDone: Catholics keep 9 March as the optional memorial of Saint Frances of Rome; in Rome her body is venerated at the church of Santa Francesca Romana in the Forum, and in some places cars are blessed on her feast because she is patron of drivers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John of God, the bookseller locked up as mad who came out to care for the sick. Your line was the hospitaller.

A woman sits down with her prayer book in a big Roman house and opens to the psalm for the hour. She reads the first line. A servant calls with a question. She marks the place, goes, comes back, reads the same line. Her husband needs her. Then a child. Then a guest. Tradition says she was called away from that one verse again and again, and every time she went without complaint. When she finally came back for good, the story goes, the verse on the page was written in gold. This is Frances of Rome.
screen: `ONE VERSE, STARTED AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `CALLED AWAY, AND GOING.` → `THE VERSE IN GOLD.`

segments.voice: Frances, tradition says, wanted from girlhood to enter a convent. Her family arranged a marriage instead, to a young nobleman named Lorenzo Ponziani. She was miserable at first. Then, with her sister-in-law Vannozza, she found her way: the two of them, in their fine clothes, slipping out to visit the sick and the poor of the city. The marriage became a long and loving one, and she raised her children in it. Then came hard years for Rome: war, famine and plague. Frances turned the family house into a place of care, gave away the household's grain and wine, nursed the sick, and, tradition says, buried one of her own children in the plague. A mother in mourning, still out in the streets. A saying handed down from her, often put this way, sums her up: a married woman must sometimes leave God at the altar to find him in her housekeeping. That's the gold verse in a sentence. Prayer never mattered less to her; serving was prayer by other means. In the Douay-Rheims, Proverbs describes a valiant woman: "She hath opened her hand to the needy, and stretched out her hands to the poor." Later, Frances gathered women who lived that way without full vows, and after her husband died she joined them. Tradition also says she saw her guardian angel at her side, lighting her way at night, which is why she's a patron of drivers. Her holiness ran through the house, not around it.

segments.voice: Picture the people under your roof, or the ones you'd call home if you live alone, and find one small need of theirs you've been stepping around: a dish, a question, a few minutes of listening. Picture putting down whatever you're doing and going to them, the way Frances closed the book. If you pray, offer that small errand as your prayer; if you don't, just breathe.

975.title: Clement Hofbauer (15 March)
975.hook: a baker's apprentice turned priest who helped renew the Church in Vienna
975.howItsDone: Catholics keep 15 March as the feast of Saint Clement Mary Hofbauer, especially in Vienna, where he is a patron of the city, and among the Redemptorists, who honor him as a founder of their work north of the Alps.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Frances of Rome, who closed her prayer book again and again to answer a call. Your line was she left prayer to serve.

Bread can't be hurried. Flour, water, yeast, then the long wait, the dough under a cloth doing work nobody can see. A baker learns to get up in the dark, do what can be done, and leave the rest alone. Clement Hofbauer learned that trade as a young man in Moravia, in central Europe. He wanted to be a priest, but his family was poor, so he kneaded dough instead. It would be years before anything he hoped for began to rise.
screen: `BREAD CAN'T BE HURRIED.` → `A BAKER'S APPRENTICE IN MORAVIA.` → `A HOPE THAT TAKES YEARS TO RISE.`

segments.voice: Clement's road was long and crooked. He worked in a monastery bakery, tried life as a hermit, walked to Rome as a pilgrim, and finally, with help from generous strangers, studied for the priesthood. In Rome he joined the Redemptorists, a young order of preachers, and was sent north to Warsaw. There he and his companions threw themselves into a city church: preaching, confessions, a school, a home for orphans. A story is told from those years. He went into a tavern to beg for his orphans, and a man spat in his face. Clement wiped it off and said, more or less, that was for me, now what will you give for my orphans? The man was so shaken, the story goes, that he gave. Then the political tide turned. The Warsaw community was shut down and the priests sent away. Clement ended up in Vienna as chaplain to a convent of nuns, hearing confessions and talking with students, artists and writers who came to his rooms. Little of it looked like success. But those conversations helped renew Catholic life in the city, and he is remembered as a patron of Vienna. The Letter of James, in the Douay-Rheims, describes this patience: "Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth." A baker would say: the dough is rising, even if you can't see it. Clement didn't live to see his order firmly planted in Austria. It came after him.

segments.voice: Find one thing in your life that isn't rising as fast as you'd like, a project, a habit, a friendship that's still shy, your own healing, and picture it like dough under a cloth: you've done your part, and work is going on that you can't see. If you pray, hand it to God for today; if you don't, breathe, and let it rise without you for a while.

976.title: Nicholas Owen (22 March)
976.hook: a carpenter who built priest-holes in English houses and died under torture
976.howItsDone: Catholics in England and Wales remember Saint Nicholas Owen with the other martyrs of England and Wales, and the Jesuits keep his memory; visitors to some old English houses can still see hiding places attributed to him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clement Hofbauer, the baker who waited years for his work to rise. Your line was the baker of vienna.

In some old English country houses, a guide will stop beside a fireplace, a staircase, or a stretch of plain wall, and press something. A panel swings open. Behind it is a space barely big enough to crouch in. Visitors call them priest-holes, built for Catholic priests to hide in when searchers came to the door, and some of them, tradition says, were built by one small man with a carpenter's tools. People called him Little John. His name was Nicholas Owen.
screen: `A PANEL SWINGS OPEN.` → `A SPACE TO CROUCH IN.` → `LITTLE JOHN, THE CARPENTER.`

segments.voice: In Nicholas Owen's England, it was a crime for a Catholic priest to say Mass, and a priest who was caught could be put to death for treason. Families who kept the old faith hid priests in their homes. Nicholas became a Jesuit brother, not a priest, and he used his trade. He worked, tradition says, mostly at night, alone, after receiving Communion, telling no one but the household. He built hiding places so well that searchers could tear a house apart for days and find nothing: false floors, hollow walls, spaces behind chimneys, sometimes one hiding place built to be found so the real one stayed hidden. Then he was caught. After days in hiding at a house called Hindlip, hungry and cramped, he came out, tradition says, partly to draw the searchers away from the priests still hidden. He was taken to the Tower of London and tortured, hung by the wrists again and again, to make him name the houses and the priests. He never did. He died there, and was canonized with other martyrs of England and Wales. It was a cruel age on more than one side, and the Church remembers him not for hating anyone, but for keeping people safe. His trade fits. In the Douay-Rheims, the people of Jesus's home town ask: "Is not this the carpenter's son?" Nicholas Owen served God the way a carpenter can: with his hands, in silence, for other people's lives.

segments.voice: Look at your hands and turn them over, and think of what they can do that someone near you needs: fix a hinge, cook a meal, carry a bag, sew a button, hold a hand. If you pray, offer your hands to God for that work; if you don't, rest them open on your knees and breathe.

977.title: Turibius of Mongrovejo (23 March)
977.hook: a lawyer made archbishop of Lima who walked his diocese and stood up for the Indigenous people in it
977.howItsDone: Catholics keep Turibius's optional memorial in March, and in Peru and across Latin America he is honored as a model of a bishop who went out to his people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nicholas Owen, the carpenter who built hiding places so priests could live. Your line was the builder of hiding places.

A lawyer is sitting at his desk in Spain, a layman, a judge in a church court, when a letter arrives from the king. The archbishop's chair in Lima, across the ocean in Peru, is empty, and they want him in it. He isn't a priest. He writes back with reasons he's the wrong man. The reasons are not accepted. So he is ordained, made a bishop, and sent across the sea to a diocese of mountains, deserts and coast, full of people whose languages he doesn't speak. He could have run it from a desk. His desk is about to become a mule.
screen: `A LAWYER, NOT A PRIEST.` → `SENT TO LIMA.` → `THE DESK BECOMES A MULE.`

segments.voice: Turibius took the job, and then he took to the road. Tradition says he spent years of his time as archbishop away from Lima, on foot and by mule, up into the Andes and down into the valleys, to villages far from any cathedral. He slept where he could and ate what was there. He confirmed, preached and listened. And he learned. He studied Quechua, a language spoken by people he served, so he could talk with them himself, not only through an interpreter. Under his leadership the church in Lima prepared a catechism in Indigenous languages, so the faith could be taught in the people's own words. What he found on the road was hard to look at. Spanish officials and landholders were abusing the Indigenous people, taking their labor and their land, and some clergy looked away. Turibius named it. He held church councils that set rules for the clergy and pressed for justice, and he clashed with powerful men who preferred him in the capital. In the Gospel of John, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "I am the good shepherd; and I know mine, and mine know me." You can't know a flock you've never met. That was his whole method. Tradition says he died on the road, on one more visit, far from his cathedral. The Church honors him as a patron of the bishops of Latin America. His title says archbishop. His feet say pastor.
screen: `AN ARCHBISHOP ON FOOT AND BY MULE.` · `HE LEARNED THE PEOPLE'S LANGUAGE.` · `HE NAMED THE ABUSE HE SAW.` · `HE DIED ON THE ROAD.` · then, large: `I KNOW MINE, AND MINE KNOW ME.`

978.title: Dismas, the good thief (25 March)
978.hook: the man crucified beside Jesus, honored by tradition as a saint
978.howItsDone: The good thief is remembered on 25 March in some places; Catholics often pray for prisoners and those who are dying with his words, and some prison ministries take him as their patron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Turibius, the archbishop who crossed his diocese by mule to know his people. Your line was he walked it all.

Three crosses on a hill outside Jerusalem. Crucifixion is how Rome punishes rebels and criminals in public. In the middle hangs Jesus. On either side, a man the Gospel of Luke calls a malefactor, an evildoer. One of them joins the crowd's mockery: if you're the Christ, save yourself, and us. The other tells him to stop. And then, in a few short words, he asks for something. Today, a dying thief's request, and the man the Church remembers as Dismas.

The text gives us very little. Luke doesn't name him. Matthew and Mark simply call the two men thieves, and say both of them reviled Jesus. Luke alone tells it differently: one mocks, and the other rebukes him. We are getting what we deserve, he says, but this man has done nothing wrong. Then he speaks to Jesus. In the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom." He doesn't ask to be taken down, or spared. Just to be remembered. And the answer comes at once: "Amen I say to thee, this day thou shalt be with me in paradise." The name Dismas comes later, from an old writing outside the Bible, sometimes called the Gospel of Nicodemus. The Church doesn't treat it as scripture, but the name stuck, and tradition honors him as a saint. Catholics read this scene in more than one way. Some see how wide mercy is: a man with nothing to show, at the very end, hears the word paradise. Others notice his honesty first: he names his own guilt before he asks for anything. And some notice a quieter thing. On a hill where people mock, he is the one who speaks to Jesus as a king. His last request has become a prayer, which some Catholics say at the end of the day, or at a deathbed. A short prayer, from the worst possible place, and an answer for this very day.

979.title: Francis of Paola (2 April)
979.hook: a hermit whose motto was charity, who named his brothers the least
979.howItsDone: Catholics keep Francis of Paola's optional memorial on 2 April; the Minim friars, nuns and lay members who follow his rule still keep a Lenten diet all year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dismas, the thief on the cross who asked only to be remembered. Your line was remember me.

A dying king sends for a hermit. The king is Louis the Eleventh of France, powerful, frightened and sick. He has heard that a holy man in the south of Italy works wonders, and he wants one. He sends messengers, gifts, promises. The hermit, a man named Francis from the little town of Paola, doesn't want to go. He goes only when the pope tells him to. He makes the long journey to France, walks into the royal court in his rough habit, and stands at the bedside of a king who wants a miracle. What he gives him is something else.
screen: `A DYING KING SENDS FOR A HERMIT.` → `HE GOES ONLY WHEN THE POPE ASKS.` → `A KING WANTS A MIRACLE.`

segments.voice: Francis didn't cure the king. Tradition says he stayed with him, prayed with him, and helped him get ready to die in peace. Then he stayed on in France for the rest of his own life, and, tradition says, the French court kept asking his advice. To see why that matters, go back to the start. As a young man Francis went off alone to live as a hermit in a cave near the sea. Other young men came to join him, and slowly a community grew. He gave them a name meant to keep them low: the Minims. Tradition says he chose it to mean the least of all, lower even than Francis of Assisi's Friars Minor, the lesser brothers. And he gave them one word as a motto, written on their badge: Charity. Love. The Minims kept a life of Lent all year round, with no meat and plain food, not to be grim, but to stay light and free for others. Behind the name sits a line from Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus speaks of the hungry, the stranger, the sick and the prisoner. In the Douay-Rheims: "Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." The least ones are where Christ says he will be found. Francis wanted his brothers among them, not above them. Even in a palace. The hermit at the king's bed was there as the least man in the room.
screen: `HE DIDN'T CURE THE KING.` · `A HERMIT IN A CAVE BY THE SEA.` · `THE MINIMS: THE LEAST OF ALL.` · `ONE WORD ON THE BADGE: CHARITY.` · then, large: `ONE OF THESE MY LEAST BRETHREN.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself what the smallest, least noticed job around you is: the dishes nobody wants, the bin at the curb, the coworker everyone talks past. Hold one of them in mind, a least thing, done without needing anyone to notice. If you pray, offer it with the word on the Minims' badge, charity; if you don't, simply hold the task in mind.

980.title: Vincent Ferrer (5 April)
980.hook: a Dominican preacher who walked from town to town calling people to repentance
980.tomorrow: John Baptist de La Salle (7 April)
980.howItsDone: Catholics keep Vincent Ferrer's optional memorial on 5 April; the Dominicans honor him as a preacher of their order, and he is especially remembered in Valencia and in Vannes, in Brittany, where he died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis of Paola, who named his brothers the Minims, the least of all. Your line was the least ones.

Dust on a road, and a crowd coming over the hill. At the front, an old friar in a black and white habit, walking, or on a donkey when his legs give out. Behind him, people who left their villages to follow him to the next one: some singing, some weeping, some who came to watch and stayed. In the town, someone builds him a platform in the square, because the church won't hold them all. He preaches for hours. Then the crowd moves on, and he moves with it. His name was Vincent Ferrer, and the road was his pulpit.
screen: `A CROWD COMING OVER THE HILL.` → `THE CHURCH WON'T HOLD THEM ALL.` → `THE ROAD WAS HIS PULPIT.`

segments.voice: Vincent was a Dominican from Valencia, in Spain, a scholar and a teacher, and for a while a man of the papal court. His world was split. The Church had rival popes, each with his own cardinals and followers, and Vincent stood loyally by one of them. Then, the story goes, he fell gravely ill and in a vision was sent out to preach. He left the court for the road, and spent the rest of his life walking across Spain, France, Italy and beyond, calling people to repentance, to turn back to God before judgment comes. Tradition tells that people who didn't share his language understood him anyway. Saint Paul, quoting the prophet Isaiah, writes in the Douay-Rheims: "How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace." Feet, notice. Not voices. His later choice was costly: he withdrew his support from the pope he had served, so the split could be healed. His preaching also had a hard side. It came at a time of heavy pressure on Jewish communities in Spain, and historians still weigh his part in it; that belongs in the story too. He died far from home, still on the road. It closes a week of feet and hands: Frances of Rome, Clement Hofbauer, Nicholas Owen, Turibius, Dismas, Francis of Paola, and now a pair of walking feet.
screen: `A SCHOLAR IN A SPLIT CHURCH.` · `SENT OUT TO PREACH ON THE ROAD.` · `HE GAVE UP HIS POPE TO HEAL THE SPLIT.` · `A HARD SIDE TO THE STORY TOO.` · then, large: `HOW BEAUTIFUL ARE THE FEET.`

segments.voice: Think of one place your feet will carry you, the kitchen, the bus, the school pickup line, and ask what the people there would learn about what you love only from watching you, with the sound off. Choose one small thing that would say it plainly: patience, a kind word, a door held open. If you pray, ask for that; if you don't, simply keep the picture.
Vincent Ferrer. A Dominican who left the papal court to walk from town to town, preaching repentance, until he died on the road.
Your line: walking preacher. In the end, the road itself became his pulpit. Until tomorrow.
